newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco companies' suit angers Alaska governor.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco companies' suit angers Alaska governor.

text.p: A pre-emptive lawsuit filed by four tobacco companies against Alaska has convinced Gov. Tony Knowles to seek reimbursement of tobacco-related medical expenses, a spokesman said Monday.
"We're in the fight now," said Bob King, Knowles' press secretary.

"It's outrageous that the tobacco industry would try to silence the state just because we were thinking about filing a suit; but now that they've fired the first shot, I'll gladly go into the battle," Knowles, a Democrat, said in a news release.
"Frankly, I hope that this additional insult is one of the straws that helps break Joe Camel's back," he said.

More than 21 percent of Alaska high schoolers smoke regularly, compared to the national average of 13.8 percent, the governor said. And Alaska's adult smoking rate of 28.9 percent is the second highest in the nation.
The lawsuit against Alaska was filed last week in U.S. District Court in Anchorage by Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds, Loews Corp 's Lorillard and B.A.T. Industries' Brown & Williamson.
Until then, the Knowles administration had been only considering joining the 19 other states that have sued tobacco-companies to recover Medicaid and other expenses, King said.
The companies' lawsuit claims that health warnings on cigarette packs relieve them from any obligation to reimburse the state for tobacco-related medical expenses.

In addition, the lawsuit claims that any state action would violate companies' right to say that nicotine is not addictive and would "severely and adversely impact interstate commerce in the sale of cigarettes."
Meanwhile, Knowles and other state leaders were pushing for a $1-a-pack tax increase that would add to the current 29-cent rate and give Alaska the nation's highest tobacco tax.
On Monday, the opening day of the state legislative session, Knowles re-introduced a bill that he sponsored last year to impose the tax hike.

Last spring, the tax measure passed the Republican-controlled state Senate by a 17-3 vote, but was blocked from a vote in the Republican-controlled state House by Speaker Gail Phillips, who said it would have violated her "no new taxes" pledge.
